claims.text: Lower-temperature single-phase ZrB2 specimens prepared above 1700 °C are vulnerable to high-temperature oxidation.
Lower-temperature single-phase ZrB2 specimens are vulnerable to corrosion by liquid plating metals.
Zr–B and B–B interactions provide adequate bonding in lower-temperature ZrB2.
The proposed intervention is to add 1–3 wt% Si to the ZrB2 precursor before sintering.
Si-doped ZrB2 can be manufactured by inert-atmosphere sintering below 1700 °C.
The resulting material is applicable to oxidation service at temperatures up to approximately 1800 °C.
The resulting material is applicable to corrosive liquid plating-metal baths.
Adding Si produces a silica or silicate intergranular phase at ZrB2 grain boundaries.
During sintering, dissolved Si segregates to ZrB2 grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary Si oxidizes during inert-atmosphere sintering to form a thin silica-based layer.
The silica-based intergranular layer reduces oxygen diffusion into ZrB2.
The silica-based intergranular layer reduces penetration by liquid plating metal.
Low-level Si addition leaves the strong bulk Zr–B and B–B bonding intact and therefore preserves mechanical strength.
Si-doped, lower-temperature ZrB2 will have hardness and structural integrity comparable to or slightly better than high-temperature single-phase ZrB2.
Si-doped ZrB2 will have significantly greater oxidation resistance than undoped lower-temperature ZrB2.
Si-doped ZrB2 will have a lower liquid-metal corrosion rate than undoped lower-temperature ZrB2.
Standard single-phase ZrB2 requires synthesis above 2300 °C.
Both high-temperature single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature undoped specimens are vulnerable to oxidation and liquid plating-metal corrosion.
Excessive Si or more extreme service conditions may generate detrimental secondary phases or degrade mechanical properties.
The expected improvements should amount to at least 20% in both oxidation resistance and liquid-metal corrosion durability, without loss of hardness.

contradictions.description: The lower-temperature material and baseline are described as being synthesized above 1700 °C, whereas the proposed condition requires temperatures below 1700 °C and the experiment specifies approximately 1700 °C. This leaves the intended manufacturing boundary inconsistent.

The mechanism requires Si to oxidize during sintering, but sintering is specified to occur in an inert atmosphere and no controlled oxygen source or post-sintering oxidation step for forming the intergranular silica is identified.
